title: Chapter 10 — Of the Forms of a Commonwealth
paragraphs: The majority, as has been shown, have the whole power of the community naturally in them when men first unite into society. They may use all that power in making laws for the community from time to time, and in executing those laws through officers of their own appointing; and then the form of the government is a perfect democracy. Or else they may put the power of making laws into the hands of a few select men and their heirs or successors; and then it is an oligarchy. Or else they may put it into the hands of one man; and then it is a monarchy. If to him and his heirs, it is a hereditary monarchy. If to him only for life, with only the power of nominating a successor returning to them at his death, it is an elective monarchy. And accordingly, out of these forms the community may make compound and mixed forms of government, as they think good. And if the majority at first give the legislative power to one or more persons only for their lives, or for some limited time, after which the supreme power is to revert to them again, then once it has reverted the community may dispose of it anew into whatever hands they please, and so constitute a new form of government. For the form of government depends on where the supreme power, which is the legislative, is placed. It is impossible to conceive that an inferior power should give orders to a superior one, or that any but the supreme power should make laws. So the form of the commonwealth is whatever the placing of the power of making laws makes it.

By “commonwealth” I must be understood all along to mean not a democracy, or any form of government, but any independent community — what the Latins signified by the word civitas. The word in our language that best answers to it is “commonwealth,” which most properly expresses such a society of men; “community” or “city” in English does not. For there may be subordinate communities within a government, and “city” among us has a quite different meaning from “commonwealth.” And therefore, to avoid ambiguity, I ask leave to use the word “commonwealth” in the sense in which I find it used by King James the First, which I take to be its genuine meaning. If anybody dislikes it, I agree with him to change it for a better one.
